paras.text: All data and code for experiments are available at Open Science Framework https://osf.io/e4hrk/.

Our daily interactions involve interpreting relations between objects, a process central to visual perception (Hafri & Firestone, 2021). For instance, one can perceive how two puzzle pieces fit together or infer the original shape of a partially eaten cookie (Chen & Scholl, 2016; Hafri & Firestone, 2021). Additionally, a phone in a basket looks like a knife in a cup due to the same “in” relation (i.e., they are perceived as similar at the relational level because visual processing represents relations abstractly), despite the two images involving completely different objects (Hafri et al., 2024). The visual system intuitively abstracts network topological relations, like T-junctions, crosses, and holes in subway maps, enabling efficient navigation from one place to another (Yousif & Brannon, 2024, 2025). The aforementioned research has focused on the spatial relations between objects, suggesting that relational structures play a fundamental role in our understanding of the world.

One traditional approach to formalizing relational representations is through geometry. Various geometric categories have been investigated within the field of cognitive science, including basic shapes (e.g., square, rectangle, circle), Euclidean geometric properties (e.g., point, line, parallelism, angle, and symmetry), and topological properties (e.g., object topology: the number of holes, inside/outside relations, and connectivity; network topology: n-point vertex) (Chen, 1982; Chen, 2005, 2025; Elder, 2018; Elder et al., 2018; Elder & Zucker, 1993, 1994; Huttenlocher et al., 1991; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2022; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2021). The mathematician Klein advocated for an invariant perspective in considering geometric properties, emphasizing a structured hierarchy among geometries (Klein, 1893). In the domain of human form perception, Chen proposed a global-to-local functional hierarchy (i.e., ascending order of stability: Euclidean geometry, affine geometry, projective geometry, and topology) (Chen, 2005). These geometric categories possess varying degrees of stability, leading to differences in constraints when describing spatial relations between objects.

Some studies have discussed the relationship between topological structures and categorical representation. Lovett and Franconeri manipulated the distance between objects to establish topological relations, which they named touching, overlapping, and containing. Utilizing the sequence comparison task, they observed improved accuracy when these topological differences were present (Lovett & Forbus, 2009; Lovett & Franconeri, 2017). Burlinson and colleagues investigated closure in several experimental tasks, including the flanker, same-different reaction time, and visual analytic tasks. Their findings affirmed that closure can be recognized as a new perceptual category in visual displays (Burlinson, 2019; Burlinson et al., 2018). However, these tasks included multiple processing stages (i.e., encoding, retrieval, and comparison), making it impossible to isolate the stage responsible for the categorical effects. Moreover, they did not adequately control for the nontopological features of visual stimuli (e.g., area, the number of terminators), leaving the possibility that these features contributed to the observed effects. Therefore, a perception paradigm specifically designed to explore topological relations between objects was needed.

The visual search task is widely recognized as an effective methodological tool for investigating perceptual relations between objects (Hafri & Firestone, 2021; Wolfe, 2021). By presenting visual stimuli simultaneously, the visual search task avoids the confounds associated with multiple processing stage tasks. Furthermore, this task can be combined with precisely controlled stimuli to rule out alternative explanations. As demonstrated by Duncan and Humphreys, attention is more effectively guided to a target as the target-distractor (TD) difference increases (Duncan & Humphreys, 1989). Topological relations (e.g., inside/outside relation) indicate that an object is either inside or outside another, with little middle ground (Hafri & Firestone, 2021). This categorical nature of topological representation increases the TD difference, thereby enhancing search efficiency. Consequently, the visual search task is suitable for studying the representation of topological relations.

A total of 116 participants took part in this study. All participants were right-handed and reported normal or corrected vision. Participants were recruited as follows: experiment 1a (N = 20; 7 males, 13 females; age range: 21–30 years, M ± SD = 23.65 ± 2.08), experiment 1b (N = 20; 3 males, 17 females; age range: 21–27 years, M ± SD = 23.50 ± 1.61), experiment 1c (N = 20; 7 males, 13 females; age range: 18–31 years, M ± SD = 23.30 ± 2.62), experiment 2a (N = 20; 9 males, 11 females; age range: 19–30 years, M ± SD = 23.75 ± 2.65), experiment 2b (N = 18; 5 males, 13 females; age range: 19–26 years, M ± SD = 22.94 ± 1.89), experiment 2c (N = 18; 3 males, 15 females; age range: 18–25 years, M ± SD = 22.61 ± 1.91). The sample size was determined using G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2009). The assumed effect size was based on effects reported in previous topological discrimination tasks (Chen, 2005). The power analysis indicated that a sample size of 15 participants yields a power of 0.8 to detect the effects with an effect size of 0.3. All participants provided informed consent and received compensation after completing the task.

The visual stimuli were presented on a 24-inch LCD screen through the Psychtoolbox (Brainard, 1997; Pelli, 1997) based on MATLAB (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA, USA), with a resolution of 1920 * 1080 and a refresh rate of 60 Hz. Participants sat approximately 70 cm away from the screen and were required to respond as quickly as possible without sacrificing accuracy.

According to the topological perception theory, the inside/outside relations are topological invariants that remain unchanged over shape-changing transformations (Chen, 1982; Chen, 2005). Experiment 1a used a large black circle and a small white circle as the visual stimuli, which had been previously used in Lovett and Franconeri’s study. The experiment aimed to validate the categorical representation of topological spatial relations using the visual search task.

Beyond the perception of 2D topological structure, Experiment 1a involved depth perception (e.g., occlusion). Stimulus pairs 2 and 4 crossed both the boundaries of inside/outside relations and depth cues (i.e., inside relations involve occlusion, outside relations do not involve occlusion). The perceived depth resulting from occlusion might have influenced the results because occluded shapes are perceived relatively farther away (Yousif & Scholl, 2019). Experiment 1b employed line drawings (Chen, 1982; Wang et al., 2007) as the visual stimuli to investigate inside/outside relations without the confusion of depth or occlusion.

The total accuracy rate in Experiment 1c was 90.40% (SD = 5.55%). The accuracy rates for each stimulus pair were as follows: pair 1 (81.40 ± 14.26%), pair 2 (93.25 ± 6.28%), pair 3 (99.10 ± 1.62%), pair 4 (93.65 ± 4.52%), pair 5 (81.65 ± 10.50%). We employed the same design to assess accuracy rate and observed that the difference between stimulus pairs was consistent with the reaction times (i.e., slower responses were associated with lower accuracy, pairs 1 and 2, pairs 2 and 3, pairs 3 and 4, pairs 4 and 5, Ps <0.008). Therefore, there was no evidence of a speed-accuracy trade-off. By calculating the difference scores between transitions (i.e., difference 1: pair 1–2, difference 2: pair 2–3, difference 3: pair 4–3, difference 4: pair 5–4), we found that the effect was indeed more dramatic for transitions to and from pair 3: difference 1 and 2 (t = –5.225, p < 0.001), difference 2 and 3 (t = –0.862, p = 0.399), difference 3 and 4 (t = 7.498, p < 0.001). Notably, transitions to and from pair 3 (i.e., outside vs. partially contained) represent a relational change to which the visual system may be sensitive (Hafri & Firestone, 2021), rather than a “pure topology” effect. The findings showed that, after the relevant inside/outside topological category boundary was removed, performance varied systematically with metric distance, while other relational differences remained (e.g., transitions involving pair 3).

Experiment 2 investigated connectivity, another topological invariant (Chen, 2005). The connectivity was defined by spatial overlapping in experiment 2a, where two objects are connected if they share the same spatial area in a 2-dimensional view. In the experiment, two bar stimuli either overlapped to form a plus (connected condition) or remained spatially separated (disconnected condition).

By demonstrating the visual system’s sensitivity to topological relations between objects, this study contributes to the growing field of relational perception. A core claim in this domain is that visual perception extracts not only individual object properties but also some relations between objects (Hafri & Firestone, 2021; Hafri & Papeo, 2025; Kaiser et al., 2019). At the level of individual objects, connectivity is a fundamental property that defines them as connected, bounded volumes with an inside and an outside. Connected entities constitute parts of a larger object (e.g., a bicycle’s wheels and frame), while disconnected entities form groups rather than objects (e.g., a flower arrangement or a flock of birds) (Cavanagh et al., 2023). At the level of visual scenes, relational representations between objects could also be formalized through geometric frameworks (e.g., physical relations such as surround involve inside/outside relations; support, balance, and attach embody the concept of connectivity; event relations like intrude and deform are shape-changing transformations). In summary, topological properties (e.g., connectivity, inside/outside relations) not only define individual perceptual objects but also the relations between objects.

Empirical evidence from vision science has revealed several critical characteristics of relational perception. First, relational structures influence scene interpretation. For instance, changes in containment or size relations between a person and a car can lead to different scene interpretations, such as vehicle breakdown, playing with a toy, or daily commuting (Summerfield et al., 2020). In the current experiments, elements presented within the four quadrants were identical in each trial. However, changing the topological relations between the elements had a significant impact on task performance. These results confirmed the critical role of some relational information in understanding visual scenes.

Secondly, the visual system spontaneously and rapidly represents the relations between objects. In exp 1a, participants irresistibly perceived the small white circle and the large black circle as having either inside or outside topological relations. Response times were significantly faster when the stimulus pairs differed in topological relations (i.e., stimulus pairs 2 and 4). The results aligned with previous findings using the brief exposure task, which found that topological properties could be extracted from exposures as short as 5 ms (Chen, 1982), suggesting the rapid processing of topological properties.

Furthermore, Kosslyn describes two distinct types of spatial relation representations in human vision: abstract categorical (i.e., the general properties of spatial structures by mapping configurations to broad equivalence classes) and specific coordinate spatial relations (i.e., indispensable for processing more precise information regarding the spatial location of objects) (Kosslyn et al., 1989). Topology focuses on properties (e.g., inside/outside relations, connectivity) that remain invariant over transformations, rather than the precise metric information (e.g., orientation, distance, and size). The current study found that task performance improved when the differences in relations crossed the boundaries of topological categories, providing evidence that topological relations were categorically represented (Burlinson, 2019; Lovett & Franconeri, 2017).

paras.sec_title: 4.2 Functional hierarchy in human form perception
paras.text: The design of visual stimuli in the current study was inspired by the seminal work of Lovett and Franconeri (2017), which manipulated the distance between objects to create different topological relations (Lovett & Franconeri, 2017). However, the current study differed from their work in several aspects. Lovett and Franconeri used the sequential same/different task, in which participants were required to report whether the first display differed from the second display. The first display was followed by a 1000 ms delay (i.e., 250 ms mask and 750 ms blank screen), which imposed high demands on participants’ short-term memory capacity. In contrast, the current study adopted the visual search task, which has been widely used in studies of the direct perception of relations between objects (Hafri & Firestone, 2021; Hafri & Papeo, 2025), such as physical instability (Yang & Wolfe, 2020), and social interactions (Papeo et al., 2019). Therefore, the present findings provide evidence for the robust representation of topological relations in visual perception.

paras.sec_title: 4.2 Functional hierarchy in human form perception
paras.text: Chen (2005) proposed a global-to-local functional hierarchy in human form perception. Consistent with this framework, the current experiments support a privileged role for topological properties in the representation of spatial relations (i.e., across six experiments, task performance was consistently modulated when the stimulus pairs crossed topological category boundaries, whereas distance effects emerged only after the relevant inside/outside topological category boundary was removed). Taken together, these findings indicate that whether a task involves changes in topological properties plays an important role in determining task performance. The priority of topological processing is further reflected in stimulus pair 3, which could also be interpreted as involving a symmetry relation (i.e., “left” vs. “right” within the large circle). However, the present results showed that reaction times for conditions involving symmetry relations (pair 3) were slower than those that differed in topological categories (pairs 2 and 4). In Lovett and Franconeri’s study, the relative priority or fundamentality of topological properties versus symmetry relations could not be distinguished (i.e., their results showed that accuracy for Interval 1 was comparable to categorical changes). The current findings, in turn, suggest a hierarchical account of human visual perception in which topological properties have a privileged role.

paras.sec_title: 4.2 Functional hierarchy in human form perception
paras.text: Meanwhile, the representation of shape (e.g., topology) reflects the core difference between cognition and computation (Chen, 2025). While numerous behavioral studies have demonstrated the importance and uniqueness of human shape perception (Chen, 1982; Chen, 2005; Elder, 2018; Elder et al., 2018; Elder & Zucker, 1993, 1994; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2022), computational models exhibit distinct representational patterns. For instance, Baker and Elder utilized animal silhouettes as visual stimuli and disrupted the object configuration while preserving local features. This manipulation influenced human task performance but did not impact deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs), suggesting that neural networks are insensitive to object configuration (Baker & Elder, 2022). Similarly, Sablé-Meyer et al. used a geometric intruder task to examine how Euclidean geometric properties are represented. They found that a convolutional neural network for object recognition reflects baboons’ performance, but an additional symbolic model was needed to account for human performance (Sablé-Meyer et al., 2021). Consequently, the underlying mechanisms of shape representation distinguish human cognition from artificial neural networks.

The visual search task used in the present study is a topological discrimination task. In target-absent trials, all stimuli were topologically equivalent; conversely, in target-present trials, the stimulus in one quadrant differed topologically from the others. Studies on topological discrimination often adopt the configural superiority effects, which emphasize that the structural relationships between components, rather than the components themselves, are more important in visual perception (Chen, 2005; Pomerantz et al., 1977). Compared with differences in individual line segments, differences in the topological structures formed by combining the line segments (e.g., the presence of a hole) facilitate discrimination (Chen, 2005). Moreover, some configural superiority effects previously reported (Eidels & Townsend, 2010; Pomerantz, 2003; Pomerantz & Pristach, 1989) may be attributed to topological structures, such as connectedness or closedness. These studies on topological discrimination provide a topological framework for characterizing perceptual relations between objects.

The topological change detection task involves shape-changing transformations. In the multiple objects tracking task, Zhou et al. found that compared with changes in other features or colors, alterations in topological properties during object motion impaired task performance, indicating that topological changes disrupt the representational continuity of perceptual objects (Zhou et al., 2010). Using a temporal order judgment task, Song et al. found that participants perceived topological changes earlier than nontopological changes. This finding supports the priority of topological changes in temporal order perception and provides evidence for attention capture by topological changes (Song et al., 2025). Furthermore, Wei et al. found a topological interference effect in a color visual working memory task. Although shape was a task-irrelevant dimension, the topological difference between the encoding and probe stages impaired color memory performance, suggesting that the visual system automatically encodes topological properties (Wei et al., 2021). In sum, these studies indicate that the visual system automatically prioritizes topological representations, highlighting their critical role in perceptual organization and attention capture.

This study has several limitations. First, the present study focused on two types of topological properties (i.e., inside/outside relations and connectivity), but did not examine holes. Nevertheless, prior work has shown that holes are also categorically represented (Burlinson, 2019; Burlinson et al., 2018), thus the current findings provide complementary evidence for the categorical representation of topological properties. Second, a key strength of the present study lies in the stimulus design which manipulated topological relations by varying the distance between two objects equally. However, this design inevitably introduced potential influences of perceived object numerosity because topological properties play a foundational role in defining perceptual objects (He et al., 2009; He et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2010). For example, in Exp 2a, stimuli 3 could be perceived as a single perceptual object, whereas stimuli 2 could be perceived as two perceptual objects. This limitation reflects a trade-off between maintaining equidistant changes in distance and controlling the number of perceptual objects (i.e., Yousif and Brannon held the number of objects constant while altering topological relations, which resulted in doubled distance differences, see Yousif & Brannon, 2025, Figure 2). Future studies could adopt alternative stimulus design strategies to disentangle changes in object numerosity from changes in topological relations. Third, the present study primarily focused on comparisons between adjacent stimulus pairs. This is because each target-present trial contained only a single stimulus pair, with strict control over distance manipulations. Future studies could design dedicated experiments focusing on more distant stimulus pairs to examine their differences in perceptual representations.
